https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: A standing ovation, a mea culpa — but now more difficult questions
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
They put a giant piece of soundproof glass across the public gallery of the House of Commons 20 years ago, after someone threw a condom full of purple flour at Tony Blair.
If it had ever crossed their mind that one day something like this might happen, they would never have done it.
Actual members of the public, looking down upon the chamber and rising to applaud what they were witnessing. It’s surely never happened before and may never again.
Perhaps the first and last politician ever to receive a standing ovation from the public gallery was John Glen, the paymaster-general . He had just announced the details of the vast compensation scheme for victims of the infected blood scandal.
If they themselves were victims, they had chosen not to wear the black, red and yellow insignia of their decades-long campaign.
The day before, the gallery had been so full of them it could have passed for the Sir Elton John stand at Vicarage Road.
They’d heard a solemn apology from the prime minister. He promised to pay them “whatever it costs” to seek to right four decades or more of having been so unimaginably wronged.
Here they were witnessing what appeared to be that promise actually being delivered.
Absolutely no sound permeates that glass.
Normally it prevents MPs from hearing various expressions of disgust hurled their way, but not today. It has silenced Extinction Rebellion, it has silenced Fathers for Justice. It has never before silenced actual gratitude.
Mr Glen was setting out the dry intricacies of how, when and why the money will be forthcoming. How various public bodies will interact with each other, who will chair what and what they will do, are never the easiest things to follow.
Each step in the process, each chain in the command, seems only to create more opportunities for obfuscation, for bureaucratic difficulty. It has proved so before and may do again.
At first glance, the government has given the campaigners what they asked for. A new authority, to be chaired by Sir Robert Francis, a KC with decades of expertise in medical litigation.
Living victims will be eligible to claim. The dead will have compensation paid to their estate. But not just that. Parents and children, even siblings, will be able to make claims of their own, to recompense not just for trauma but for losses suffered in their own lives, which were put on hold to care for others.
The grand scale of the mea culpa, the cartoonish size of the blank cheque was welcomed, but it invited difficult questions. For the second day in a row, Dame Diana Johnson MP, Westminster’s outstanding campaigner on this issue, was far more interested in the details than the grand gestures.
If Francis’s unique insight is suddenly so valued, why were two of his more recent proposals, as published in interim reports by the Infected Blood Inquiry, ignored until now? If he’d been listened to this time last year, significant payments could already have been made. He wasn’t, and they haven’t.
Some of the questions MPs felt they must politely ask still retained the capacity to shock. The father of the house, Sir Peter Bottomley, inquired as to whether some kind of “NHS passport” might be set up for infected blood victims.
The point of this would be to stop them “constantly being asked the same questions” by doctors. The treatments for hepatitis C destroyed patients’ livers. Now, every time they go to hospital, or to their GP, they find themselves being asked how much they drink, over and over again.
Rishi Sunak wasn’t there, by the way, because he’d gone to Austria instead, for a meeting with Austrian chancellor Karl Nehammer. The choreography of it all had been agreed far in advance. The two men held a joint press conference, to sing the praises of “third country deportation schemes.”
Nehammer thinks the EU should be copying the UK’s Rwanda plan.
Twenty-four hours had not passed since the prime minister had been standing at the despatch box of the House of Commons, making stern promises in his best solemn staccato that “nothing like this can ever happen again.”
Whatever one’s views on Rwanda, however seemingly intractable the problem of illegal migration, it’s not debatable that the prime minister has spent a very long time trying to find ways to get around the various human rights laws that have thus far prevented him from filling up planes and sending them off to Rwanda in their thousands.
The Supreme Court has said it’s not safe.
The House of Lords has said the same and he’s ignored them. They might be wrong but there are many people in Westminster, right now, warning that something “like this” may be about to happen.
“Nothing like this can ever happen again.” How long is never again? It would come as a shock to precisely no one if it turns out to be less than a single day.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Rewrites, God jokes and the Diane dilemma: inside Labour’s war room
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
It was last Sunday night that word reached Morgan McSweeney, Sir Keir Starmer’s campaign chief, that he might have to cancel his holiday to prepare for a snap election. The low-profile Irishman had been through the adrenaline-depleting ritual of rumour, excitement and disappointment before.
This time it felt different. Intelligence was emerging from the shadow cabinet. David Lammy was at a private dinner with Yulia Navalnaya, widow of the Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny, when a senior Tory texted to say it was on. A sudden surge in activity on the betting markets sealed McSweeney’s conviction that a July poll would be called imminently.
Yet as late as Wednesday morning, when the pair met in the House of Commons, Starmer himself remained sceptical. The Labour leader repeated like a holy mantra to staff that there was a plan. He was comforted by the dress rehearsal offered by the recent local elections. But he was still unpersuaded that Rishi Sunak would go early. He knuckled down, writing his script for prime minister’s questions, focusing on the contaminated blood scandal.
It was a characteristic display of caution from a man determined not to get ahead of himself. After a first 48 hours in which Sunak’s launch was blighted by rain and the SNP leader’s plane was diverted by fog, one Tory peer ruefully joked that even God had defected to Starmer’s party. A Labour strategist’s response to such gallows humour: “I think he’s still undecided.”
That riposte cuts to the core of Starmer’s strategy, which is a blend of vaulting ambition — even the Almighty is a target voter — and risk averseness. He believes the electorate is far more volatile than ever. He is also haunted by Labour’s record of losing elections it seemed destined to win, often because of its weakness on the economy.
In 2010 Ed Miliband was criticised for adopting a 35 per cent strategy squarely focused around mobilising the party’s core vote.
Starmer is seeking a far broader coalition: polls point to double-digit leads in every region, which, if converted into votes on July 4, could translate to a 1997-style deluge. Staff have been told the approach is akin to the tweet composed by the World Wide Web creator Sir Tim Berners-Lee and beamed around the Olympic opening ceremony in 2012: “This Is For Everyone.” Starmer — a hyper-competitive five-a-side player who this year met his hero Arsène Wenger for a private dinner — is keen to adopt a similar winning mentality.
For that reason the party has adopted a one-word slogan that means different things to different voters but has the widest possible resonance: Change. In England, that means change from the Conservatives; north of the border from the SNP.
To flesh out the message, the party wants to provide digestible examples of the difference Labour would make.
Rachel Reeves is the key “message-carrier” here. The shadow chancellor is the personification of the party’s desire not to offer a variety of change that is either too radical or undeliverable in the eyes of an electorate, which, according to its research, is more cynical about political promises than ever before. The proposed remedy for Tory “chaos” is a combination of economic stability and policy offers aimed squarely at the cost of living crisis. Hence the decision to rewrite and rebrand Labour’s package of workers’ rights reforms.
This weekend The Sunday Times revealed the party had junked the “New Deal for Working People” — of which Angela Rayner had been the architect — and replaced it with the more consumer-oriented “Labour’s Plan to Make Work Pay”. Hours later Reeves visited an Iceland supermarket to make her case.
Starmer chose to launch his campaign in Gillingham, one of Kent’s Brexit-backing Medway towns and the kind of Tory seat he wants to flip. Labour last won the constituency, where the Tories have a 15,000 majority, in 2005. For months the party was refreshing draft “grids” for the campaign, but the idea was always to launch in the southeast of England before travelling to Scotland, which Starmer sees as vital to any majority.
The desire to appeal across the board does not mean the party is not focused on specific kinds of voters and seats. Deborah Mattinson, Gordon Brown’s former pollster, has long championed the idea of the “hero voter” — potential Tory-Labour switchers who voted Brexit, are socially conservative and do not live in big cities.
McSweeney is similarly focused on winning voters without degrees. Yet he does not want Labour to repeat past mistakes by funnelling resources to cities where its victory is assured, or obsessing over one kind of imaginary voter. He wants the party to stay the course, remaining outside its comfort zone and striking a balance between targeting and retaining broad appeal to the last. In his eyes Labour has a tendency to lose focus as polling day approaches, comparing previous iterations to a friend at the pub who claims they are going to compete in the Olympics, only to down a pint of Guinness and lose interest.
That means funnelling campaign staff and volunteers from groups such as Labour Together, the Starmerite think tank, and Arden, a lobbying firm set up by the former Scottish Labour leader Jim Murphy, as widely and deftly as possible.
To do this, Starmer expects to draw upon an election war chest which, thanks to Tory reforms, can spend up to £35 million. One of his first acts after PMQs on Wednesday was to meet David Evans, the party’s general secretary, who assured him the finances were in rude health. For this, he is particularly indebted to Lord Alli, a millionaire peer and friend of Sir Tony Blair once described as one of the few openly gay Muslim politicians in the world. Alli has headed up fundraising and told the shadow cabinet last week that there would be enough cash to reach the ceiling. Those who have already contributed include Gary Lubner, the Autoglass founder, Stuart Roden, a hedge fund manager, and Dale Vince, a green energy industrialist who stopped funding Just Stop Oil in the face of Tory attack. The main unions will also contribute.
Such funds meant that, before the election was even announced, Labour had expanded its office space in Southwark, southeast London. They were ready on the ground too: back in March, Hollie Ridley, McSweeney’s deputy, armed candidates in every marginal with a “break in case of emergency” packs for a snap poll containing posters, leaflets, garden boards and digital adverts. She also told them to record what would appear spontaneous announcements welcoming news of an election — all of which went live instantly last week. Back at headquarters, the plan is that at 6.30am every day the core of the campaign team led by McSweeney will meet there, with Starmer able to dial in remotely when needed. Others in the room include the husband and wife duo Pat and Marianna McFadden — the former an MP who served as Blair’s political secretary and is now campaign co-ordinator, the latter an alumna of the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change and now deputy campaign director. Sue Gray, Starmer’s chief aide, is involved but will also continue to oversee preparations for government.
Despite the vivid visual metaphor offered by Sunak’s rain-soaked launch, Starmer’s aides have sought to resist any schadenfreude. They are happy to go for the prime minister personally — Reeves herself reminded voters on Saturday that he was richer than the King, according to the latest Sunday Times Rich List — but do not want to be seen to be delighting in his misfortune and know there will be a wobble of their own at some point. Their hope is not to avoid any mistakes at all — the leader knows that is all but impossible — but to ensure the message of the campaign is sufficiently strong it cannot be eclipsed by one gaffe.
The party has also adopted a risk-averse approach to events that could wrongfoot Starmer or undermine the strategy. The party is in talks with broadcasters about leader and deputy leader debates, but has already made clear Starmer will take part in only two live contests.
As for the manifesto, it is expected to be thin. The leader will announce a handful of punchy policies but otherwise hammer home the change message. His team is also not averse to repeating existing measures, believing as they do that many voters have long since switched off from politics and will have little detailed knowledge of its plans on energy and the cost of living.
In response to the criticism that he has not yet offered a Big Idea, an aide to Starmer was nonplussed, pointing to proposals on housebuilding and Great British Energy. “We believe in big ideas but not ideas that can’t be delivered,” they said. Such thinking guided the belated decision to limit the party’s employment reforms, which no longer include a proposed ban on zero-hours contracts or an increase in statutory sick pay. Ditto removing the wider package from the party’s core messaging with the exception of Scotland, where they played especially well in last year’s Rutherglen & Hamilton West by-election, which Labour seized from the SNP.
Alongside change, the other c-word is Corbyn. Last week he announced he would stand against Labour in his Islington North constituency, prompting his immediate expulsion from the party. Starmer’s team are perfectly comfortable to draw a contrast between the two if necessary, having done so to great political advantage since suspending him from the party in 2020.
Another quasi-opponent on the left is Diane Abbott, who has been suspended from the parliamentary party for a year and remains under investigation for comments comparing antisemitism to discrimination experienced by “redheads”. Starmer’s instinctive approach has been to purge Corbynite opponents. But he is unsure about whether to let Abbott stand.
Starmer is conscious of her record as Britain’s first black female MP and knows a number of his MPs have qualms about her situation. At the same time many around him believe Abbott to be unpopular with voters they are seeking to convert, and she is known to have published an autobiography that attacks him in uncompromising terms. The situation must be resolved by June 4, in less than a fortnight’s time, when the party’s ruling national executive committee meets to rubber-stamp candidates interviewed and vetted under emergency procedures.
The party otherwise sees the left as a subplot to the campaign, rather than the existential concern that defined Starmer’s first two years as leader. The local elections especially vindicated his belief that the coalition of Muslim voters, Corbynite leftwingers and young progressives who have opposed his position on Gaza are not going to blow his strategy off course.
For now, Starmer is said to be adopting the same approach he did towards the idea of a snap poll itself: extreme caution coupled with an ambition that, until polling day, will not speak its name.

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: Don’t scorn students for believing in a cause
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
Outside the LSE a small but noisy group performs a call and response to a woman holding a megaphone. “No to f***king genocide. Palestine will be free.” Members of the encampment at nearby King’s College have come to show solidarity with those sleeping in a scattering of tents in the LSE foyer. “The students united will never be defeated…”
So much is familiar to me. The serious overseas students for whom a cause has real-life consequences, the fashionable white kids with edgy haircuts, the activists greeting each other with delirious hugs, the polite Revolutionary Communist Party guy handing out leaflets about class struggle, the blithe majority strolling to lunch without a glance.
At Sussex University in the early 1980s I spent weekends on marches, took part in occupations, made placards, organised meetings — so many interminable meetings — and, like Greta Thunberg, wore a keffiyeh. That the Swedish environmentalist has adopted a Palestinian scarf is said to signify how every issue from LGBT rights to Gaza has now been mushed into a single “omnicause”.
But it was ever thus. Radical activism has always been a multipack deal. Our omnicause encompassed apartheid, Nicaragua, nuclear disarmament, the miners’ strike and that Thatcher-era hardy perennial, The Cuts. Palestine-Israel was then, as now, the most divisive and bitterly contested — though, of course, 19-year-old me thought I had it all figured out.
Outside the LSE, a man stands slightly apart from the protest, an Israeli student listening to the slogans: will they chant “from the river to the sea” or go full pro-Hamas? (Neither today.) He loathes Netanyahu and believes the students’ demands for divestment are feeding Bibi’s narrative that the world is against Israel, keeping his populist coalition in power for ever so the war never ends.
“Why, instead of engaging with the Israeli left,” he asks, “do students align with the Arab right?” When Jewish students put up October 7 hostage photographs they were torn down in minutes: “What other cause would the university allow to occupy a building for weeks?”
Indeed, the camp appears to be regarded by LSE management as a sort of living art installation. An administrator just gives a students-will-be-students shrug when I ask about it. As I chat with a charming Jordanian, who claims the camp includes many supporters of a two-state solution, a woman hands him two full Sainsbury’s bags: “I’m a staff member,” she says, “and want to donate this.” Humanitarian relief for kids camping indoors, five minutes from a Pret.
It’s easy to laugh. Throughout history students have been ridiculous, idealistic, passionate, privileged, solipsistic, self-righteous, exasperating and sometimes — from the Prague Spring to Tiananmen Square — outstandingly brave. You can ask why they care about Gaza as they didn’t about Assad’s crimes in Syria, or you can scorn Queers for Palestine when Hamas lobs gay men from roofs. But as bombs still pound cornered civilians in a wasteland racked with hunger and disease, when Israel presses on impervious to universal horror, what is wrong with students being society’s nagging conscience and demanding it stop?
In the US, Robert Reich, a lawyer and academic who worked for Carter, Ford and Clinton, writes that President Biden felt no domestic pressure on Gaza before the student protests. But camps at Ivy League colleges such as Columbia created a “moral urgency” which emboldened him to withhold heavy weapons for use by Israel in Rafah.
Some of my generation condemn today’s students as a threat to the West, beguiled by extremists. Expel them without degrees for besmirching college lawns! I can’t join in, not least because we were worse. At Sussex we occupied a science building, keeping engineering students from lectures. We slept on the admin block floor, singing Beatles songs and, filled with revolutionary euphoria, had disastrous one-night stands. Anarchists painted a horrible mural, provoking a rare comrade who cared about inconveniencing campus workers, to cry “you call it art, I call it a bloody mess, get it cleaned up!”.
Most painfully now I recall a union debate on the motion “Zionism is racism” with Jewish students, some from Holocaust survivor families, making emotional speeches. But I voted for it anyway. Things are so simple when you’re young. Craving to belong, you pick a team, buy into a world view. Maturity makes you pragmatic, more tolerant and appreciative of nuance but also nihilistic — nothing changes, so why even try? Unlike us, today’s student protesters aren’t fighting their institutions: tutors don’t try to get them expelled but send bags of food. Likewise Extinction Rebellion is full of middle-aged road-blockers, while eightysomethings try to vandalise the Magna Carta. Protest has kudos now and grown-ups — whether parents or lecturers — can be too fearful of being cancelled to give the counter view.
On Israel-Gaza, universities should enable dialogue rather than shut it down. The LSE encampment, I’m told, held standing-room-only lectures on the Middle East. Did those who believe Israel has the right to exist and defend itself feel able to speak? There is great hunger to understand — but rarely the courage to present a full spectrum of views.
What did our 1980s protests achieve? Thatcher was re-elected, The Cuts didn’t stop, the miners lost. But apartheid fell thanks in part to pressure applied by the world’s young. Student activism engaged thousands in politics for life: some ended up in government. Now it feels the young cannot win. They are denounced if they stay at home preening on TikTok. But if they care about something enough to organise, sit through boring meetings and sleep in a tent during exam week, they are just dupes sucked into an omnicause.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Just Stop Oil should be banned like terror groups, report says
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.subtitle: A government-commissioned report recommends limiting groups such as Palestine Action to crack down on disruptive protests
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Protest groups like Just Stop Oil and Palestine Action should be proscribed in a similar way to terror organisations, a government-commissioned report will say.
Lord Walney, its adviser on political violence and disruption, is recommending that the government creates “extreme protests restriction orders”.
His report, which makes 40 recommendations, is set to be finalised and sent to No 10 as soon as Monday.
Walney has also held discussions with senior Labour figures and hopes the party will be sympathetic to his ideas.
It comes amid a growing debate about the acceptable limits on protests, with ministers saying they want to clamp down on overly disruptive demonstrations.
Walney wants to make it an offence to belong to a protest group judged to be “extreme” and which routinely uses criminal methods to campaign.
The move would be part of a wider effort to make it harder to fundraise or organise for certain groups which use mass disruption and promote targeting individuals or businesses.
In a copy of the draft report, seen by the BBC, Walney said: “Militant groups like Palestine Action and Just Stop Oil are using criminal tactics to create mayhem and hold the public and workers to ransom without fear of consequence. Banning terror groups has made it harder for their activists to plan crimes — that approach should be extended to extreme protest groups too.”
The idea is viewed as a tool rather than a panacea to tackle protests that the government deems disruptive and extremist.
There are concerns that proscribing one protest group could just lead it to morph into another but Walney believes it would still be a useful tool. There are also concerns that current police powers to arrest people if they break the Public Order Act are leading to delays in the matter going to trial.
Due to a backlog in the courts, critics of the “extreme” protesters believe they are acting with relative impunity, given their case might not be heard for several years.
Other recommendations Walney will make as part of the report include banning activists from holding protests near defence manufacturing and energy sites.
Palestine Action attracted particular scrutiny after it targeted the sale of British-made weapons to Israel. This month it launched an assault on UAV Tactical Systems, a drone manufacturer, in Leicestershire.
The group posted afterwards on Twitter/X: “Whilst one group smashed a lorry into Elbit’s Leicester drone factory, another scaled the roof of the building. Collectively, they’ve shut down the Israeli weapons maker.”
Given concerns about the use of such tactics, Walney’s report will say: “The government should consider ways to ensure resilience of production for defence and energy companies whose operations are being disrupted by illegal protest.
“This could include setting a protective buffer zone around certain sites or expediting injunctions on certain protesters not to enter such a zone.”
In response to the plans, Just Stop Oil said ministers were the “dangerous radicals that are endangering all of us” through their climate policies.
Palestine Action told the BBC that most British people sympathised with its call for an arms embargo between the UK and Israel. The group also said the proposals would not deter its campaigning.
Government sources were receptive to the ideas but stressed they would reserve judgment until the final report was published.
A Home Office spokesman said: “Extremism of any kind has no place in our society and we will not tolerate tactics that set out to intimidate, threaten or cause disruption to the law-abiding majority.
“In recent months we have also witnessed a small number of protesters display violent and hateful behaviour, and the police have our full support in tackling extremism and hate crime. We are considering the report’s recommendations extremely carefully and will respond in due course.”

Groups which cause severe disruption should be proscribed, the report will say

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: Arrested in our 80s over Magna Carta: meet the Just Stop Oil pensioners
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
“Jesus was an activist, no doubt about it,” the Rev Dr Sue Parfitt says from a flowery armchair in her quaint cottage in Bristol. The octogenarian looks up to her mantelpiece at a wooden figure of Christ on the cross. “He broke the law continually and in the end was arrested and executed for it.” In the armchair opposite, Judy Bruce, 85, a retired biology teacher, smiles wryly.
A quiche may be warming in the oven, but Bruce and Parfitt aren’t here for a polite ladies’ lunch. A week ago they were arrested after the display case of Magna Carta at the British Library was chipped with a hammer and chisel. They held a banner that declared: “The government is breaking the law.” The act was carried out on behalf of Just Stop Oil (JSO). Bruce and Parfitt were both arrested and charged with £2,000 in criminal damage.
Since JSO was founded in 2022, its headline-grabbing stunts of civil disobedience — which it calls “actions” — have become a familiar sight. The climate group has managed to unite most of the country in irritation. Orange paint, soup and powder has been sprayed everywhere from snooker tournaments and art galleries to tennis matches and universities.
So why are two respectable elderly women, a reverend and a teacher, risking getting arrested in the name of the climate?
Over a cup of tea (with oat milk), and with Parfitt’s cats Holly and Mistletoe at their feet, the pair explain how they got into radical climate activism.
Parfitt, 82, was raised a Christian by conservative parents in south Wales. She read history at Bristol University and was briefly involved with the peace movement in the late 1960s but stopped because she feared being arrested at such a young age.
“It’s a different matter getting arrested in my eighties,” she says, matter-of-factly. “The point is to make the best use of your latter years. And what could be a better use than trying to save humanity from extinction?”
After stints as a nun and a family therapist, Parfitt married an Anglican priest and trained as one herself. When her husband died in 2013 she joined Christian Climate Action, which has since become the de facto Christian wing of Extinction Rebellion.
Bruce came to activism later in life, after retiring from teaching biology in a private school and moving to Swansea. She remembers always showing concern for things such as the ozone layer and GM crops, but became involved with Extinction Rebellion after her partner, who she says would have disapproved of her being arrested, died in 2020.
“When I first heard of doing actions that would end up with arrest, I thought, ‘Oh no. I don’t want to do that. Bad people do that!’ ” She was involved in a march during the G7 summit in Cornwall in 2021, but was motivated to break the law after “realising that non-arrestable ways of doing things are not making any impact at all”.
They don’t exactly fit the classic profile of radical activists: Parfitt walks with a cane and Bruce is very slight, in a blue cardigan with pearl buttons. But both talk passionately about the climate crisis with a steely determination.
Bruce tells me she and Parfitt met “sitting in front of an oil tanker” in April 2022 and teamed up again at the suggestion of JSO when they unfurled a banner during a thanksgiving service at St Paul’s Cathedral that read: “Will our children thank us?”
“I think they had the idea that these two oldies might drum up some interest,” Parfitt says with a chuckle.
But they draw the line at some stunts. They turned down a suggestion to break the glass covering the Rokeby Venus painting in the National Gallery, chosen because it had been slashed by the suffragette Mary Richardson in 1914. (Two other JSO activists were arrested after it was vandalised in November and have pleaded not guilty to causing criminal damage.)
Parfitt’s background as a historian means she wants to ensure any painting or historical document will not be damaged. “There was no question there was any risk to Magna Carta, nor would we want there to be,” she says.
“We’re incredibly law-abiding citizens — believe it or not,” says Bruce.
Parfitt, still a practising Anglican priest, says the Church isn’t “terribly happy” about her involvement. “I have to report to my bishop every action I take,” she says.
Parfitt and Bruce know their actions rub people up the wrong way: they have lost friends and had fractious exchanges with family members. Bruce has been manhandled by a passerby. The two say they are vilified online and called “arthritic old codgers”, as Bruce puts it. “Well, I am arthritic,” Parfitt says with a laugh.
Both say the ageism they experience makes them feel sad rather than hurt. Parfitt says that as well as challenging perceptions of 80-year-olds, she wants to challenge their own age group too. “I often say to my friends, ‘Why don’t you come and do this, what have you got to lose?’. I don’t have grandchildren, but I say to people, ‘I’m doing this for your grandchildren’.”
But is it working? JSO floundered last year as its biggest donor, the green energy tycoon Dale Vince, announced he was cutting the cash supply, admitting that no amount of protesting would stop the government from North Sea drilling.
Are Bruce and Parfitt aware their actions may have alienated the public? They agree that climate activists can come across as preaching and self-righteous,“but in what other way is it possible to influence governmental action?” asks Bruce. “If we don’t do things that annoy people, it doesn’t get into the news.”

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: The electric car crash will rival the dotcom bubble
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
Ministers can’t get out much these days without being heckled, especially by green campaign groups such as Just Stop Oil. So no surprise that last week the secretary of state for energy security and net zero, Claire Coutinho, struggled to make herself heard above the din of demonstrators in the hall as she delivered a speech at a business conference.
Her message was definitely not what those demonstrators wanted to hear (though they aren’t in the listening business). Coutinho criticised what she called the “net zero leviathan of central planning” and said that products designed to meet this target should not be “forced on British consumers”.
In one respect the quietly formidable Coutinho has been as good as her word. The government has postponed by ten years (to 2035) the deadline after which households will be forbidden to install any new gas boilers. And last month Coutinho delayed, though only by a year, a policy of fining manufacturers for missing targets for the installation of heat pumps.
But in another respect there is a gaping chasm between the government’s rhetoric about the primacy of consumer choice “on the road to net zero” and its actual policies. This concerns the product most beloved of British consumers and on which they — we — have the strongest opinions. I refer, of course, to the car. Although Rishi Sunak, in September, moved from 2030 to 2035 the date by which all manufacturers would be required to stop selling any new vehicles that were not purely electric, the elaborate system of penalties remained fully in place. So, this year, manufacturers are obliged to ensure that at least 22 per cent of their sales are of EVs, and for each and every non-electric car sold that breaches the target, they are liable to a fine of £15,000. The thing ratchets up every year, so that by 2030 their sales must be at least 80 per cent EVs (not even hybrids qualify), or else …
When it became clear Sunak would postpone the 2030 deadline (one of Boris Johnson’s vainglorious attempts to demonstrate Britain’s leadership in the “battle against climate change”), a number of manufacturers upbraided the PM. Ford UK’s chief, Lisa Brankin, remonstrated: “Our business needs three things from the UK government: ambition, commitment and consistency. A relaxation of 2030 would undermine all three.” Stellantis, which owns Vauxhall, Peugeot, Citroën and Fiat, issued a statement warning that “clarity and reasonable anticipation are important”.
Seven months on, the company’s horn is sounding a very different note. Ten days ago its chairman, Carlos Tavares, said the law fining companies for selling cars that did not meet the EV quota was “terrible for the UK”, and that “I’m not going to sell cars at a loss”. The reason for Mr Tavares going from volt to volte-face is clear for all to see (now). Or, as he put it, EVs were “crashing in the world of reality”.
To no sensible person’s surprise, consumers have been deterred by a combination of higher purchase prices, “range anxiety” and plummeting resale values, largely due to increasing awareness of the prohibitive costs if the battery needs replacing. The Stellantis boss now concedes that the “natural” market share for EVs in the UK is about half what he is being required to sell under the regulations, which are starting to bite (indeed, taking great munches out of his company’s profit margins).
In other words, this is exactly the sort of “forcing” of products onto the consumer that Coutinho says the government shouldn’t be doing. This is not a British problem alone. The EU has an almost identical policy, yet in Germany the European election manifesto of the centre-right Christian Democrats declared: “We want to abandon the ban on combustion engines and preserve Germany’s cutting edge combustion technology.”
As things stand, China will be the only winner. It, uniquely, is able to sell EVs more cheaply than the equivalent combustion engine models, and is about to flood European markets. The EU will soon be forced to choose between its vaunted commitment to fighting climate change and the existence of its own car manufacturing businesses.
If only it — and our own government — had listened to Akio Toyoda. In January the chairman of Toyota (grandson of its founder) told employees in a Q&A session of the company’s booming sales of hybrid vehicles, and pointed out: “Customers and the market will decide, not regulations or political power.”
This has now dawned on one of the world’s biggest car leasing companies, Hertz — and its shareholders. Last week its share price fell by a quarter as it announced a sell-off of many thousands of Teslas that it had only recently acquired, absorbing a thumping loss. And Tesla itself has just announced it will be dumping 14,000 employees, with Elon Musk firing his entire team responsible for its “supercharger network”. What we are witnessing is an imminent business catastrophe impelled by a global corporate stampede: the herd was galvanised by governments, which have yet to recognise, let alone admit, their own responsibility.
In terms of global misallocation of capital, there has been nothing like it since the dotcom bubble. As far as the UK is concerned, the obvious thing for the government to do is to live up to Claire Coutinho’s words and abandon the attempt to force consumers to buy products they don’t entirely trust, which can only end terribly for the businesses involved.
However, it is not so simple. The problem is the commitment to make the UK “net zero” by 2050, a declarative piece of legislation insouciantly passed without proper debate in the dying days of Theresa May’s tenure of office, as her “legacy”. It means any successor government is liable to legal challenge if it makes decisions that can be construed as breaching that commitment.
And groups such as Friends of the Earth are highly experienced litigants in such matters. Indeed, only last Friday the High Court found in FoE’s favour, and against the government, over the green lobby group’s claim that ministers had not provided sufficient evidence that their existing policies would achieve net zero by 2050, as they are legally required to do.
So whenever a minister suggests a policy change that might be viewed as in breach of the net zero commitment, the civil servants involved immediately warn that it may be open to legal challenge or judicial review.
Not that such a scene is ever likely to take place when, as is generally expected, Ed Miliband takes over Coutinho’s job in a Labour government. Then we will see the “net zero leviathan of central planning” she warned against. My money is on consumers, all the same. Because they are also known as “voters”.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Far-left groups trying to undermine UK, says anti-extremism tsar
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.subtitle: Lord Walney does not rule out proscribing Just Stop Oil and Palestine Action ‘which clearly break the law to force the conversation’
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Far-left groups are seeking to “undermine” Britain’s democratic principles by refusing to comply with the law, the government’s political violence tsar has warned.
Lord Walney, a crossbench peer who was asked by ministers to investigate domestic extremism, said there had been a “really important” focus on violent Islamist and far-right groups which pose a threat to Britain.
But he said the risk from the “extreme far-left seeking to undermine institutions and the basic democratic principles that have underpinned our country for many years” had been “underappreciated”.
Walney’s report is due to be released this week. On Sunday he did not rule out a recommendation that organisations such as Just Stop Oil and Palestine Action be proscribed in a similar way to terrorist groups.
Other recommendations include that protest groups compensate people whose lives they disrupt by, for example, holding up ambulances, causing losses for businesses or preventing students attending lectures, the Daily Telegraph reported.
Walney told Sky News: “When you look at organisations who use criminal tactics as a means — very deliberate means — to try and force the conversation towards the kind of change they want rather than engaging in our democratic channels, I think it does ask questions.”
Asked specifically about Just Stop Oil and Palestine Action, he said: “Both of the those organisations are clearly breaking the law as a way of trying to force the conversation. I think we should be less relaxed about that.”
He said: “These organisations have not yet been judged to meet the terrorist threshold — which is clearly defined and the home secretary has to rule on — but there is that space where if organisations are clearly using criminal tactics, they are not being deterred by the individual offences that their activists are being charged with, but proscription has worked in the terrorist context to be able to restrict the activities of certain organisations. It’s not perfect but it can be an important tool.”
The report also follows regular protests over the conflict in Gaza in London and elsewhere in the UK. Thousands of people joined a march on Saturday and police made seven arrests. Those held included a demonstrator seen carrying a coffin with offensive language on it and a man who appeared to lead an offensive chant and damage a traffic light.
Walney told Sky he had been concerned over “many months that the police do seem limited in what they’re able to do to balance people’s right to protest with the cumulative impact of having marches through central London on a weekly or very regular basis”.
He said the demonstrations were “making substantial parts of the community, sizeable parts of our Jewish community in London, apprehensive at best about going into the centre of the city”. He added: “There has been a substantial level of criminality and disorder and antisemitic content around the margins of the marches.”
Palestine Action and Just Stop Oil accused Walney of having conflicting interests. He is the chair of the Purpose Business Coalition, an organisation run by the PR and lobbying firm Crowne Associates, which counts the oil company BP and the arms company Leonardo among its clients.
Palestine Action said: “Palestine Action takes direct action in order to disrupt the production of Israeli weapons on British soil, preventing their use against the Palestinian people. To claim Mr Woodcock [Walney] is an ‘independent’ adviser and to allow him, a paid lobbyist, to suggest British policy on this topic is a mockery of our democracy.”
Just Stop Oil said: “It would be a disgraceful deception of the public for anyone to present those recommendations as ‘independent’. His ill-thought through and self-serving recommendations do not serve the public good. The readers of The Times can draw their own conclusions.”
Walney said: “Over the three years that I have conducted this review I have consistently applied an objective standard and sought a wide range of perspectives, including through a formal call for evidence and analysis of public opinion through polling exercises.
“I now look forward to the publication of the independent analysis and recommendations in my extensive report. My non-parliamentary interests are declared as required and past positions held are a matter of record.”
Walney said the intense pressure over the conflict also led directly to democracy being “under strain and under threat” with the targeting of MPs.
He said: “We’ve got lawmakers who are facing violent threats and intimidation on a daily basis. You talk to MPs and you look at some of the available figures at the way that levels of public protection funding has been soaring in recent months.
“So you have a level of threat and intimidation that is being placed on MPs … through the extreme elements of pro-Palestinian protesters, you’re having council meetings disrupted.“
The latest MP to be targeted by protesters is Siobhan Baillie, the Conservative MP for Stroud, Gloucestershire, who had effigies of blood-soaked babies left outside her office.
Demonstrators began by peacefully chalking on the pavement but the next morning Baillie’s staff found effigies of babies covered in fake blood.
Baillie said: “It’s another example of how vile and polarised discourse has become in this country. Like most people I am appalled by the loss of life in Israel and Gaza and yearn for an end to hostilities through a ceasefire deal that all calm heads understand will take both sides to agree.
“Attacking backbench MPs will not help a single innocent child caught in this dreadful conflict and yet again it is a female MP who is targeted, I am the third female MP to have effigies of dead babies delivered to their doorstep.”
Walney said: “Many people talk about this as an extension of our democracy rather than what it is — unacceptable attempts to coerce and intimidate lawmakers and the public.”
The Home Office said: “The right to protest is a cornerstone of our democracy but there are clear concerns about the cumulative impact protests are having on some of our communities which we are looking at.
“All communities should be able to go about their daily lives without fear. We have been clear with the police that they must use all the powers available to them to police protests appropriately. [They] will always have our backing in doing so.”

https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.title: Shell faces shareholder revolt over climate strategy
https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.subtitle: Investors rebuke company over plan to water down emissions reduction targets
https://www.thetimes.com/business-money/.text:
Shareholders have publicly rebuked Shell over a plan to water down its emissions reduction targets, as the company faces scrutiny by investors and wider society over the speed of its plans to make the transition to cleaner energy.
In March, Shell weakened a 2030 carbon reduction target and scrapped a 2035 carbon intensity reduction objective, citing expectations of strong demand for gas and uncertainty about the energy transition. However, it reaffirmed a plan to cut emissions to net zero by 2050.
Almost 22 per cent of shareholders voted against the climate strategy at its annual meeting. A opposing vote of more than 20 per cent requires Shell to explain how it intends to consult shareholders about their views and ­to report back within six months.
Wael Sawan, who was appointed as chief executive of Europe’s biggest oil and gas company at the start of last year, is trying to boost returns and close the valuation gap with Shell’s American peers.
The meeting was delayed and disrupted by protests from environmental campaigners, who interrupted the opening remarks of Sir Andrew Mackenzie, the chairman of Shell, by shouting “Shell kills, Shell kills, Shell kills, Shell kills” to the tune of the Dolly Parton song Jolene.
However, Sawan, 49, said shareholders had “strongly backed” the company’s strategy to “deliver more value with less emissions”.
Sawan said: “Our focus on performance, discipline and simplification enables us to invest in providing the energy the world needs today and in helping to build the low-carbon energy system of the future.”
Maja Darlington, a campaigner at Greenpeace UK, who was among the protesters, said: “Since taking over a year ago, Sawan has slashed Shell’s already weak climate targets and even some of the company’s biggest shareholders are unsettled by his approach. The world can’t wait for fossil fuel giants like Shell to reform themselves.”
A resolution urging Shell to align its “medium-term” carbon reduction targets with the 2015 Paris climate agreement, including reducing emissions from fuels burnt by Shell’s consumers, was defeated. Just over 81 per cent of shareholders voted against the resolution, which was led by Follow This, an activist shareholder.
The Paris agreement included a goal to substantially reduce global greenhouse gas emissions to hold the increase in average global temperatures this century to well below 2C, and ideally to 1.5C, above pre-industrial levels. Last year was the warmest since global records were first kept in 1850, with almost half of days being more than 1.5C warmer than the 1850-1900 average.
Norway’s £1.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund, Shell’s second largest shareholder, said it would reject the resolution before the meeting. It said Shell should make “additional disclosures that could reduce uncertainty” about the company’s approach to climate change. Norges Bank Investment Management has a stake of about 3 per cent in Shell.

https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/cele.title: How I got to know my cousin ‘Ran’
https://www.thetimes.com/life-style/cele.text:
In the 1980s, when the actor Joseph Fiennes was at secondary school, he used to hear rumours about his glamorous Old Etonian cousin, the explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes. The pair hadn’t yet met. Joseph wasn’t sure he wanted to.
“There I am at my south London state school and all I hear about is Ran and his Eton friends getting arrested by the police, so I was thinking, ‘Maybe private school isn’t all it’s cracked up to be’,” he recalls.
Joseph, now 53, was a teenager when he first heard how “Ran”, his third cousin once removed (Sir Ranulph and Joseph’s father, Mark, shared a great-great-grandfather), had once plotted a bomb attack on the set of the 1967 film Dr Dolittle, starring Rex Harrison. An Old Etonian friend of Ranulph’s was furious that the film’s set had spoilt the Cotswolds village (Castle Combe in Wiltshire) where he lived. Ranulph, then serving with the SAS, offered to blow it up.
“Stupid, because we were caught and I received six months’ probation and a big fine. However, it had just won the award for the prettiest village in England,” Ranulph, 80, explains.
“In a sense you were an early eco-warrior?” Joseph asks.
“Perhaps, but they didn’t call us that. They called us idiots.”
There was another story that impressed Joseph, star of Shakespeare in Love, who is fresh from playing the football manager Gareth Southgate in the Olivier-winning play Dear England. This one was about his cousin scaling Lupton’s Tower, a building at Eton College dating from Tudor times.
“Mine was the first ascent by night from the eastern side,” Ranulph confirms proudly. “Later, Bear [Grylls, the explorer and fellow Old Etonian] did it, claiming it was harder because the school had erected barbed wire defences. But, of course, that made it easier because barbed wire gives you something to grab hold of.”
Welcome to the extraordinary world of the Fienneses. Despite not meeting until a family gathering in 2000, they are now firm friends. Today, we meet on the 14th floor of their publicist’s London office to discuss an extraordinary journey they have made together, recreating a 2,400km river expedition from British Columbia’s northern border to Vancouver, which Ranulph originally undertook in 1971 — a four-month odyssey by rubber dinghy involving perilous rapids that had never previously been completed.
This time he and his cousin took it a bit easier: travelling by foot, road, boat and air for three weeks, all of it filmed for a two-part National Geographic documentary called Return to the Wild. That’s because, having been diagnosed with Parkinson’s roughly five years ago, the world’s greatest living explorer (according to Guinness World Records) isn’t as mobile as he once was. Despite this, he remains a commanding presence, cutting off his cousin’s memory prompts with a “yes, that’s quite enough, I’ve got it now”.
A toned, smiley Joseph is undeterred. During a poignant scene in the documentary, he calls Ranulph his “hero” as they look at photos taken on the original 1971 expedition.
“I think of that bloke — me, back then — as someone totally different, because I’m now deaf, not blind but getting that way, and into an age where my runs become shuffles,” Ranulph says. “When I see these, it reminds me that, in those days, we thought we could do anything.”
The pair first travelled together in 2018 when they recreated Ranulph’s 1968 expedition to Egypt (he travelled the River Nile by hovercraft). “The only way to really know this extraordinary man is to journey with him,” Joseph says. There was a deeper emotional reason for Ranulph wanting to return to Canada. “My wife Ginny [who died of stomach cancer in 2004] drove a support Land Rover full of petrol and whisky,” he recalls.
“I don’t think my wife would drive a Land Rover full of whisky solely for my benefit,” says Joseph, who is married to the Swiss-Spanish actress and model María Dolores Diéguez.
On screen, it’s clear the actor’s “dad” jokes are as much of a challenge to the grizzled explorer — who famously sawed off his frostbitten fingertips after a trip to the Arctic — as the threat of a black bear attack or falling down a ravine. “Do you do this just for the krill of it?” he wisecracks, as Ranulph tries to catch a fish.
“Overall, Joe’s comedy made it all very jolly,” says Ranulph today, staring straight ahead, bushy eyebrows twitching.
But Parkinson’s disease means the Canadian adventure is also tinged by sadness. He is clearly not the man who circumnavigated the world on its polar axis by land or who, in 2003, ran seven marathons on seven continents in seven days, four months after suffering a heart attack (he required a double heart bypass operation).
• Sir Ranulph Fiennes on breaking records and life with Parkinson’s
These days, he has to take seven pills a day and concentrate carefully when walking. “My concentration is bad,” he admits. “You desperately want to say a word like ‘suicide’ or ‘love’, a feeling, and the word just goes.”
Has he been thinking about suicide?
“I haven’t considered suicide in terms of doing it myself, but when asked my opinion on it, I found I hadn’t really got one,” he says.
In Canada, on medical advice, it is Joseph who does all the rowing and climbing. He even abseils into a crevasse.
“Nothing like Ran’s exploits,” he says. “It was all very safe. For me the most moving part of the experience was having a chance to know the man who was mythical to me growing up. Yes, Parkinson’s means he faces challenges. I feel he is looking back and perhaps understanding what drove him to these incredible feats.”
There is a moving scene where First Nation people conduct a ceremony to ensure safe travel for the pair. They talk about communicating with their ancestors before Ranulph describes how he draws on the voice of his father (also called Ranulph) in adversity.
On his 97-day journey across Antarctica in the 1990s, for example — during which temperatures dropped to minus 90C (contemporaneous reports described him as emerging “more dead than alive”) — it was the voice of his father that drove him on. Ranulph Sr died during the Second World War, four months before his son was born.
“But because of all the stories my mother told me, he is in me,” Ranulph says. “I only ever wanted to make him proud and not give up.”
Given that he never met his father, strictly speaking the voice in Ranulph’s head is his own?
“It’s what I imagine my dad would say,” he says. “A voice that tells me, ‘Don’t give in, don’t be weak’.”
It seems an odd question to ask a man now stroking his chin with sawn-off finger stumps, but has Ranulph actually enjoyed his expeditions?
“Perhaps I did focus too much on being first and getting from one place to another,” he muses. “But the thing with expeditions is the sponsors want you to be first. That’s how you get the money: be first. And I didn’t want to let my father down, to think he might be ashamed.”
There is something poignant about Ranulph’s drive compared with Joseph’s ease. In 2009 Ranulph became the oldest British person to climb Everest (at 65) despite suffering from vertigo.
“The best cure for vertigo is heights,” he says. “To be honest, I thought I’d conquered it but when I was climbing a ladder at home to clear leaves from the gutter recently, it came back.”
He has raised more than £19 million for various charities over the course of his career but the self-sacrifice seems to be part of the point. When I visited his home on Exmoor ten years ago, where he lives with his second wife, Louise, and their 18-year-old daughter, Elizabeth, he was annoyed that one of his sawn-off fingertips, kept in a drawer in his office, had gone missing. Did it ever turn up? “Joyce, my PA, and I agree that a mouse probably ate it,” he says.
Men have changed and so too has exploration. Ranulph used to navigate using his wristwatch and the position of the sun. Now, we have geolocation and Google maps, but he is having none of it.
“This is the most modern bit of tech I own,” he asserts, handing me a battered brick phone with his mobile number sellotaped to the back.
“That’s great, Ran,” Joseph says. “I fear the smartphone has robbed us of our intuitive smartness.”
Maybe wildlife programmes have had an effect too. When they encounter a black bear, Joseph has to remind himself he’s not in a Disney film.
“It was a very cute looking bear,” he says, shrugging. “And you have to remember, we have consumed hours and hours of wildlife on TV. But when you see one in the wilderness for real, you have to balance a sense of wonder with danger.”
“When I went to the Arctic, the Canadian government warned me that 10 per cent of polar bears eat humans,” Ranulph recalls. “I said, ‘How do I tell which ones? Do I have to bloody ask them?’”
• Joseph Fiennes: how I turn myself into Gareth Southgate
Of course, that wilderness is under threat, as we see when Joseph abseils down a crevasse on the fast-disappearing Athabasca glacier. Would either of them ever endorse eco-activists such as Just Stop Oil?
“I’m glad a lot more people are trying to stop the destruction of forests and the climate,” Ranulph says. “I would be vocal but probably not stop traffic.”
“The Athabasca glacier will probably be gone in my lifetime,” Joseph says. “We are at a tipping point so we do need to be conscious but also active. So, yeah, I would stop traffic. I should stop traffic, although what we need is change at governmental level.”
The pair are clearly fond of each other. Joseph is adapting Ranulph’s 1997 thriller The Sett (where an accountant takes on the mafia, the CIA and the gangland underworld after the murder of his family) for the big screen. But will there be another joint adventure?
“Can we tell him?” Joseph asks.
“No, or the Norwegians might do it first,” Ranulph says, referring to his toughest adversaries over the decades. In fact, when I visited him ten years ago, he had a radio mast erected in the garden to eavesdrop on their expedition plans.
“If you come second, nobody cares,” he says, sharply. “Norwegians are a nuisance in that respect.”
Back in Canada at the end of their trip, fishing for sturgeon, which can live for upwards of 150 years, Joseph asks his cousin if he’d like to live that long. Yes, Ranulph says, he’d like to see how certain things pan out.
Like what, for example?
“The end of Putin and all the autocrats like him. I want to see everyone agree that peace, democracy and love will get you through life.”
“That’s so beautiful,” Joseph says. “And if anyone can make it to 200, it’s you.”Fiennes: Return to the Wild starts on National Geographic on Sunday, May 26, at 8pm

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: First migrants bound for Rwanda detained in Home Office raids
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.subtitle: Deportation flights are scheduled to take off by July after disputed legislation became law last week
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Women were among the first migrants detained for deportation to Rwanda in a series of raids in the four nations of the UK.
More than 800 immigration enforcement officers were involved but officials refused to disclose how many migrants had been detained because of fears doing so would undermine operations.
Senior officials overseeing the raids, code-named Operation Vector, said those detained since they began on Monday lunchtime posed little resistance. They have pursued the most compliant among a group of 5,700 migrants eligible for removal to Rwanda and officials expect to face more resistance as the operation continues.
Protesters attempted to obstruct officers by lying in front of their vans in locations including Swansea, Salford and Croydon, south London. Just Stop Oil protesters attempted to disrupt operations at immigration offices in Solihull and police made ten arrests.
As the first migrants were detained on Monday and Tuesday, 400 migrants crossed the Channel in eight boats, taking the total this year to 7,567, a record for the first four months of a year.
The Home Office accepted it faced a series of legal hurdles to get the first migrants on a plane by July. Officials said they had begun detaining migrants this week because they expect people to submit complex legal challenges. The FDA, the trade union that represents senior civil servants, announced it had began legal proceedings against the Rwanda policy.
Officials also said they expected that some people might have to be released from detention before the first flight, raising the risk of them absconding. Migrants can be detained only if there is a realistic prospect of their removal, meaning they could be released if they have a strong case for fighting removal or for other reasons such as being vulnerable to detention conditions. Judges will make the final decision.
The Home Office insisted anyone released would be subject to strict bail conditions. It also said it would have to stop or slow down the detentions once the seven immigration removal centres were full, placing a cap on numbers to be deported. There are only a few hundred places available for migrants identified for deportation to Rwanda out of a maximum detention capacity of 2,200.
A source close to the home secretary said: “We are focused on the operationalisation of the Rwanda scheme and we’ll continue to do so. We’ve long been aware some people will use a variety of forums to try to disrupt that. In the meantime, we will continue to deliver on the timeline set out by the prime minister.”
In footage of some of the raids published by the Home Office, officers were seen entering terraced houses and leaving with a man in handcuffs. He appeared to be wearing pyjamas and a hoodie, and is understood to have been living in Coventry. Two other men were taken away in Peugeot vans with a cage in the back.
Photos published by the Home Office show officers equipped with an “enforcer”, the term used for the battering rams used by the police to gain entry to locked premises. However, officials said they had not yet needed to use the device.
Eddy Montgomery, director of enforcement at the Home Office, said the department was minimising details disclosed to the public to ensure detentions could be done at a larger scale. He said: “Our specialist operational teams are highly trained and fully equipped to carry out the necessary enforcement activity at pace and in the safest way possible. It is vital that operational detail is kept to a minimum, to protect colleagues involved and those being detained, as well as ensuring we can deliver this large-scale operation as quickly as possible.”
On Tuesday, Kemi Badenoch, the business secretary, said Rwanda was a “holiday” destination after the first migrant was relocated to the country on a separate voluntary scheme. The failed asylum seeker, of African origin, was paid £3,000 to move to Kigali voluntarily on Monday. Rwanda is increasingly becoming a tourism destination, with 1.4 million visits each year, including 4,258 holidaying in the country in 2019.
The FDA said it had submitted an application for a judicial review against the Safety of Rwanda Act on the basis that the controversial legislation, passed last week, contravenes the civil service code.
The union said that powers granted under the act for a minister to ignore an injunction from the European Court of Human Rights, known as a Rule 39 order, conflicted with the duty of civil servants under the code to act in compliance with international law.
Dave Penman, the general secretary, said: “Civil servants should never be left in a position where they are conflicted between the instructions of ministers and adhering to the civil service code, yet that is exactly what the government has chosen to do.
“This is not an accident, or down to poor drafting. It’s a political choice from the government, made not for the good of the country but to avoid upsetting either of the warring factions within its own party. It’s also irresponsible. Those seeking to undermine the integrity and impartiality of the civil service have seized on the difficulties the government has had in implementing this policy, to accuse civil servants of acting politically.”
What happens next?
Those detained were served with notices informing them that their asylum claim was inadmissible because they could now be removed to a safe third country.
They were taken to one of seven immigration removal centres, where they will be kept until the first flight leaves in nine to 11 weeks, unless they succeed in being bailed.
They will be given a phone call after 24-48 hours once they are in the detention centre, where they get the chance to contact a lawyer on taxpayer-funded legal aid.
Individuals will be given eight days to submit reasons why they are unsuitable for removal to Rwanda but they must supply accompanying “compelling evidence” that they would face “serious and irreversible harm” by being deported.
This is their only avenue for challenging their initial deportation notice following the Safety of Rwanda Act, which restricts appeals to the country being unsafe for their individual circumstances.
If there is no submission, the Home Office will continue with their removal directions.
The Home Office will respond to a submission challenging their removal within two days of receiving it, according to leaked documents setting out the timeframe.
If a person wants to continue to fight removal, the legal action starts in earnest, instructing lawyers to submit a judicial review on their behalf. Legal action will have to be submitted within 23 days and it will then be heard at either an Upper Tribunal court or the High Court.
It will then be for a judge to determine whether to grant a full hearing or an injunction that may suspend their deportation pending a full hearing.
If unsuccessful, the person will have an opportunity to take their case to the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg. This is the ultimate arbiter of the European Convention on Human Rights and before the first scheduled flight in June 2022 it granted an interim measure — known as a Rule 39 order — to suspend the flights until a full hearing had taken place in the UK’s domestic courts.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/scotland/art.title: Robin Harper: Why I left the Green Party
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/scotland/art.subtitle: As the Scottish Greens expel 13 activists for believing ‘sex is a biological reality’, Robin Harper explains why he left the party he used to lead
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/scotland/art.text:
The sinking of the Greenpeace ship the Rainbow Warrior in Auckland harbour in 1985 instilled in me a sense of urgency about how we treat our environment. I joined Greenpeace, Friends of the Earth and the Scottish Ecology Party and never looked back.
I was happy in the company of the Edinburgh branch of the Ecology Party, which back then had 30 members, of whom about a dozen were active. We met over bread and cheese suppers and listened to each other, working on policies based on the best scientific advice available at the time.
Fast forward to the Scottish parliament elections in 1999. After 14 years of campaigning, standing in every local council by-election, as well as in two Westminster and two European parliamentary elections, I was selected to fight for the second votes of constituents of the Lothians region for the new parliament at Holyrood. I was the co-convenor and principal speaker of the party.
As the only Green member of the first Scottish parliament for nearly 300 years, I had much to do.
In my first year, I gave talks, including 70 keynote speeches, to 41 environmental organisations, 40 social and community organisations, 51 schools, colleges and education groups, 22 business organisations and 11 art and architecture organisations.
I co-chaired four cross-party groups and served on the transport and environment committee and petitions committee. I kept up this gruelling pace for another three years and stood again for the Green Party in the 2003 election, when we returned seven MSPs. Two days after the election, I took a phone call from Jack McConnell, the first minister, asking if I would like to come to Bute House to discuss the possibility of us working together.
My strong preference is for working in collaboration for the greater good, rather than confrontation for point-scoring and grandstanding, but my new colleagues had other ideas. I will never know whether this was a missed opportunity.
My personal pleasure at our success was seriously dented a day or two later when succession planning was top of the agenda at our first post-election meeting. I had to sit and listen for 30 minutes while members solemnly discussed how soon I could be replaced, referring to me in the third person throughout. It was insensitive and demeaning, and although I never mentioned it, I struggled under a bit of a cloud for the next eight years.
Over the past three years, the Green Party has embarked on a relentless journey into unreality. The setting of a ludicrously ambitious climate change target that was clearly no more than a publicity stunt; the hubristic recycling scheme, designed to prove that Scotland knows best; the unrealistic banning of gas and wood-burning boilers with no recognition of the nature of Scotland’s existing housing stock; the freeze on rents with its unconsidered negative consequences for the market — everything the Greens touch now turns to dust.
My personal tipping point was the introduction of the gender recognition legislation. It was clearly rushed through parliament ahead of the Cass report for the simple reason that the findings might undermine the need for the legislation.
It was painful to watch almost every amendment fall with little discussion as the bill passed through a stacked committee. I felt strongly that it was imperative to see properly peer-reviewed scientific studies before embarking on legislation that set vulnerable young people on irreversible pathways, but when I discussed this concern with my local Green councillor, he reported me to the party’s conduct committee.
All I wanted was to put the case for delay. This was represented as breaking the party’s rules and I risked being expelled. Long gone indeed were the days when party members sat around and discussed policy issues with openness and passion, and everybody’s opinion counted. Once I had dealt with the initial feeling of hurt, incomprehension, dismay and eventually anger at my treatment, I made up my mind to leave.
These days I would prefer to be devoting all my energies to assisting the group Our Scottish Future, set up by the former prime minister Gordon Brown. As it is, the ever-present danger of the trans lobby gaining any more of a foothold than it already has in Scottish politics demands a bigger share of my attention than I would wish. Trans people deserve respect in our society, but not at the expense of women’s rights, or anyone else’s rights for that matter.
I would like to make a wake-up call today. We have an established political party that not only denies free speech to its women members, it throws them out the moment they challenge party policy. The leadership is all-powerful — the ground of extreme politics. What is happening in the Green Party is also happening in other political parties and in our public services. There are strong signs that the SNP’s centralism is a first step to totalitarianism. Already in Scotland it is against the law to speak out on a range of issues, with your friends and families invited to shop you East German style if you step over the line.
Populism is a potent political weapon and all parties have active youth wings who appear to be the most vulnerable to its extremist messages. Combine snitching with a disregard for science and truth-telling and the way is open to the destruction of western democracy.
It is not old-fashioned to say that listening to other people matters, that freedom of speech matters, and that opinions can and often should be changed through rigorous discussion and debate.
Robin Harper was the UK’s first Green parliamentarian who last year resigned his life membership of the party he claims has “lost the plot”.

https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.title: Palestine puts paid to cosy campus consensus
https://www.thetimes.com/comment/columni.text:
The other day I went to UCL to watch a pro-Palestine demonstration under a louring London sky. The protesters were energetic in their chanting and drumming but I was struck by how little interest most other students showed in the small band camped on the lawn outside the university library. The protest, despite media interest, was not an exotic spectacle for students.
Perhaps this is because British universities have now seen more than a decade of protests: a radical spell longer than even the golden age of campus activism in the 1960s. I arrived at university in 2011 in the midst of the demonstrations against tuition fees. Then came the anti-capitalist Occupy movement. Then Rhodes Must Fall. Then MeToo. Then anti-Brexit marches. Then trans rights. Then Extinction Rebellion. Then BLM. Then Just Stop Oil. And myriad other half-remembered causes. There can scarcely have been a year since about 2010 when an undergraduate with radical aspirations and a spare afternoon could not have found a sit-in or march to attend.
I do not point this out to doubt the sincerity of student activists or the justness of (some of) the causes above, merely to observe that on modern campuses protest has become a kind of institution. Also notable is how little mayhem student protest has caused in 21st-century Britain. True, the sit-ins and paint-splashings look dramatic, especially when viewed in jumpy iPhone footage. And offence and inconvenience have been caused. But we forget that student protest was once a byword for wholesale social chaos. No demonstration this century has approached the violence of hurled paving stones and barricaded Parisian streets of 1968. In the same year, at LSE an elderly porter died of a heart attack as student protesters punched the outraged university official trying to come to his aid.
A decade of student protest should sound like hell for anyone running a university. But administrators have managed to accommodate themselves to the new ambient mood of political radicalism with almost suspicious ease. University leaders now speak the jargon of protest as fluently as that of grades and coursework. Student anger can simply be met with bland agreement. For instance, a student may protest that the university’s museums are colonial relics unworthy of a progressive modern institution. The museums tend to concur. The last time I visited the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford, I was greeted with signs on which the curators explained their institution was “a footprint of colonialism” and dolefully informed me that its collections “represent a lot of pain and suffering”. The museum is a protest against itself.
Indeed, many universities have even found it beneficial to adopt the language of political radicalism. As the American writer Tyler Austin Harper points out, exclusive universities looking to burnish their moral reputations have “cribbed the language of edgy politics, openly framing their institutions and initiatives as aspirationally ‘anti-racist’ and ‘decolonial’ enterprises while welcoming ‘scholar-activists’”. Scholar-activists and decolonial agendas are difficult for even the most belligerent student activist to criticise. It is probably important that while the Sixties students were in revolt against their parents’ world view, those attending 21st-century protests are not really diverging from the values they were raised with. They are likely to have studied Rosa Parks and Martin Luther King in school. In the childrens’ sections of metropolitan bookshops you can find titles like A is for Activist and No! My First Book of Protest. The production of childrens’ books about suffragettes is an industry in itself. Greta Thunberg is the subject of numerous biographies for young readers. A teacher friend was once briefly (and incongruously) assigned to run the “activism society” of a London private school.
For students raised in this cultural atmosphere, participation in a protest must seem as inevitable a rite of passage as internships and graduation. For many, the aim is not to bring down the social order but to participate in a relatively uncontroversial modern ritual. A 2017 Pepsi advert used a political demonstration as the glamorous backdrop for Kendall Jenner to wander around displaying a carbonated beverage at flattering angles. Real radicals have tended to deplore the toothlessness of modern protest movements. The Marxist writer Mark Fisher worried about the way political dissent had been blandly folded into the establishment as an unthreatening “carnivalesque background noise”.
Thus far universities have accommodated themselves to this background noise. The Palestine demonstrations present a new problem because the turbulence at its heart — incidents of antisemitism and fury at mass casualties — cannot be absorbed in the vague language of earnest radical consensus. Universities are happy to pay lip service to ideas of racial justice and concern for the environment but must be more careful when they have worried Jewish student groups and unhappy donors to think about.
This novelty perhaps explains the panicked, incoherent response, such as the (distinctly unradical) decision at Columbia to call in the police and the nervous waffle issued by UCL. “But what of our wider responsibilities?” runs one of four rhetorical questions in the university’s official statement. Universities are not used to having to disagree with their students. It is a useful lesson: protest is a more difficult and serious matter than easy radical platitudes may lead you to believe.
