https://www.thetimes.com/uk/royal-family.title: Jonathan Yeo’s portrait of King Charles — our writers’ verdicts
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/royal-family.subtitle: Giles Coren, Emma Duncan, Robert Crampton and Alice Thomson assess the painting by Jonathan Yeo
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/royal-family.text:
My opinion of the portrait is neither here nor there. Jonny Yeo is one of my oldest and closest friends. If he had killed a man, I would cover for him, say the other bloke started it, do the time for him if it came to that.
He has painted me in oil twice, the first time in 1999, the summer I turned 30. He had not done many portraits then and I wasn’t sure he had got the lips right, but I look at it now and, Jesus, it’s lovely. I’d give anything to be back on that terrace in the hills above Antibes again, reading while he painted. And he painted me again 12 years ago, when I was older, craggier. I thought he’d made me too craggy, but I look at it now and wonder, “was I ever that young?”.
Jonny’s photorealistic genius is a given. He could have painted the King like a photo on Instagram if he had wanted. But he seeks to do more. The face is incredible. Almost no one else alive can paint a face that well. I have cropped the photo on my phone down to just the head and thought how, if he had done that, only the face filling the canvas, Jonny might have impressed a wider audience more emphatically with his special gift — forced them to regard his representational talent — but that is not what he was commissioned to do. Nor is it what he is most interested in doing.
The full work is harder to grasp. It opens itself up to criticism. The King has puffy hands, Jonny has not dodged that. People fear a sense of non-completion. Jonny doesn’t care. There is a lot of red, yes. You can choose to wonder why or yodel that it doesn’t work. The butterfly was a risk, for sure. But Jonny nearly died twice (juvenile cancer, adult cardiac arrest), and his family has been torn apart by a public political sex scandal (and rebuilt itself). He didn’t get a degree. He only taught himself to paint because it looked like fun.
One morning he stands in front of a naked Sienna Miller, the next before a fully clad Tony Blair (thank God it’s that way round), and he is as relaxed as you or I would be putting the kids to bed. Believe me, whatever your opinion, he can take it.
The face is great — friendly, wise and compassionate — but the butterfly is a bit primary school. Now children, when you think of nature, what do you think of? A butterfly, perhaps? Your picture is of a nice man who likes nature, so why don’t you paint one by his shoulder?
The red is what most people will remember, though. I don’t like it. Red is a dominating colour, crowding out all other hues, so it contradicts the friendly modesty of the face. They won’t be able to hang it next to anything else. It will have to have an entire wall to itself. That would imply a self-importance which I doubt the King would want to convey.
I can’t quite fathom why Yeo made that choice. It’s the kind of thing that I would do if I liked the face and wanted to disguise the fact that the hands (notoriously difficult) weren’t really working, but Yeo is a fine painter, so I think we can ignore that possibility. Is the King covered in blood to atone for his nation’s past sins? He has edged closer towards remorse for slavery than his predecessors, but not that far. Is he in an environmental inferno? That would be more on-brand but still a bit extreme. Perhaps it’s a cunning pre-emptive move by Yeo, daubing the portrait with brightly coloured paint before Just Stop Oil does.
I can’t take the whole “official portrait” thing seriously. The ritual is one of the many anachronisms surrounding the royal family, the chief one of which, of course, is the continued existence of a hereditary monarch at all. Also, hanging a massive portrait of an individual on a wall is a weird concept anyway. I suspect the King is embarrassed by the sheer solipsism of the custom.
As a republican, I see matters monarchical through a prism of whether such-and-such a saga, morsel of gossip, argument, gaffe and, indeed, portrait, make the royals more or less popular. I’m always hoping for less. I can’t see Yeo’s effort moving the market much either way. Many people seem to like the pinky-red vibrancy. I do too, while also thinking it looks neither one thing nor the other, a bit figurative, a bit abstract, a bit collage. Like a promising second draft, not a finished product.
Artists always say that the hands are the most difficult part of the anatomy to get right. I can see why because even someone as obviously skilful as Yeo hasn’t mastered them. I know the King’s fingers are pretty sausagey, but they’re not a baseball mitt, as rendered here. Plus, while the detail of his face is exquisite, it doesn’t match up with much else on the canvas, so he looks like a game-for-a-laugh teacher at the school fete, sticking his head through a cut-out figure on a stall. Wet sponges anyone? Might not be a bad idea.
All I can see is red. It’s overwhelming, like Duchy Originals strawberry jam or the end of the apocalypse. It’s crimson, the colour of carnage, the wrong time of the month or doom.
I love Yeo’s work, but his portrait of Queen Camilla is painted in soothing blue/grey tones that I find more relaxing and less alarming in these turbulent times. The conservationist King could have been depicted in shades of green.
The monarch butterfly calms the painting a bit. And I rather like the expression on the King’s Cheshire Cat face. There’s no arrogance or petulance, just a thoughtful, tentative man who knows he bears a huge responsibility as he takes on his new role. His sausage fingers have also been kindly depicted.
“Yes, you’ve got him,” Camilla tactfully said when the King unveiled this vast work. And Yeo has, if you ignore the background. Unlike Winston Churchill, I can’t see Charles putting this portrait on the bonfire where it would merge into the flames. But the King must be relieved it will hang in the Drapers’ Hall and not in his drawing room.

image.caption: From left, Robert Crampton, Giles Coren, Emma Duncan and Alice Thomson evaluate the portrait that will hang in the Drapers’ Hall
